challenge: The EWARS repo's 'weekly' example data is not usable as weekly development data
solution: Kept as a smoke test only; weekly development uses Nicaragua weekly data (JC-01)
details: `example_data/` has a `week` column but month-formatted `time_period` values (2023-05 ... 2023-12), 13 locations and 8 periods, with the derived columns (`Cases`, `E`=200000, `ID_year`, ...) precomputed. It is too short for a backtest with lagged covariates.

challenge: The R reference needs Docker, the Docker daemon is not running, and R-INLA is amd64-only on an arm64 Mac
solution: Open: the human starts Docker Desktop before batch 2; the reference runs under amd64 emulation and its slowness is recorded
details: `docker info` returned 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon'. The EWARS Dockerfile pins linux/amd64 on both stages because R-INLA has no arm64 Linux build.

challenge: No data-specific licence for the example datasets
solution: Treated as distributed under the licences of the repositories that ship them (GPL-3.0, AGPL-3.0); to be re-checked by /release
details: No LICENSE, README or DESCRIPTION in chap-core `example_data/` names a licence for the data (`DESCRIPTION` there is an unfilled R-package template).

challenge: The chap-core clone (65 MB) is too large to commit
solution: `Archive/chap-core/src/` is gitignored; it can be re-obtained exactly from the commit in its provenance.md, and its checksum manifest is committed
details: The plan's storage rule: archived clones over about 50 MB are gitignored and re-obtainable.

challenge: predict.R loads `sf` and `spdep`, but no call to either was found
solution: To confirm in batch 3 by a full read; if they are unused, the Python port needs no spatial-geometry counterpart
details: A grep for st_*, poly2nb, nb2* and sf::/spdep:: found nothing. The spatial effect is `iid`, which needs no adjacency graph.

challenge: The period formats differ: predict.R parses weeks as '...W<nn>', while chap-core's weekly CSVs use date ranges ('2003-12-29/2004-01-04')
solution: To settle in batch 2: observe exactly what chap passes to the service for weekly data
details: predict.R:158-162 derives `week` from `sub('.*W','',time_period)` when neither `week` nor `month` is present.

challenge: The R original fails inside INLA on its own monthly example data when chap backtests it
solution: Diagnosed from the failed job's workspace: chap forecasts the file's pre-derived `month` column as a covariate, R uses it as-is, INLA rejects the near-duplicate cyclic positions. Inputs reduced to the data contract (JC-05)
details: INLA error: `Locations are too close for f(ID_time_cyclic, model="rw1", ...): min(diff(sort(x)))/diff(range(x)) = 8.074e-17 < 1e-06`, on the first predict of the first split. The workspace chapkit kept (`results/diagnose_monthly/failed_predict_workspace/`) shows historic.csv with integer months and future.csv with `month` = 10.00000000000001, 10.999999999999986, 12.000000000000018: chap's default `climatology` provider regresses every non-target column on month of year for the forecast window. predict.R only derives `month` from time_period when no `month` column exists. The same file reduced to the six contract columns runs (`outcomes.txt`). The weekly Nicaragua file carries only contract columns and ran unchanged. Not an anchor failure: the model runs through chap on data shaped as its README specifies.

challenge: A chap model-configuration YAML that omits `additional_continuous_covariates` runs EWARS with no climate covariates
solution: The covariates are always listed in the YAML (JC-06); the tutorial says why
details: ModelConfiguration.additional_continuous_covariates defaults to [], and `_chapkit_config_payload` always sends it; the service treats [] as 'no covariates', not as its default list. Nothing warns. Found by reading chap_core/models/external_chapkit_model.py before the first run, so no run was affected; it matters for the batch-4 config variants and for any reader of the tutorial.

challenge: The first reference run stopped after the first failed evaluation instead of continuing
solution: PS4 without a command substitution; the aborted attempt's outputs kept in results/run1_attempt1_aborted/
details: The scripts run under macOS /bin/bash 3.2 (the fresh shell). With `set -e`, a PS4 containing `$(date ...)` made the shell exit right after `cmd || rc=$?` recorded a failure; reproduced in isolation. Timings come from timings.tsv instead.

challenge: The R reference cannot be seeded through chap: predict.R sets no seed and chap passes none
solution: Accepted: chap-level R runs are not reproducible exactly; the L5 noise floor (batch 4) is measured from repeated unseeded runs, and seeds are set in the R instrumentation scripts for L3–L4
details: grep finds no set.seed or INLA `seed` argument in scripts/*.R; the config schema has no seed field. rnbinom and inla.posterior.sample therefore draw from R's time-seeded RNG. Plan §4 (Project seed) anticipated recording 'whatever seeding chap and the image allow': here that is none. The tutorial check prints the EWARS CRPS of two independent runs as a first look.

challenge: Resolution of CH-02 (Docker not running)
solution: Docker Desktop running (server 27.4.0, linux/aarch64); the amd64 image runs under emulation; per-evaluation times in results/run1/timings.tsv
details: CH-02 stays as raised; this entry records its resolution, since the ledger is append-only.

challenge: Resolution of CH-06 (weekly period format)
solution: chap passes weekly periods to the service as ISO-like `YYYY-Wnn` (e.g. `2004-W01`); predict.R takes the year from characters 1–4 and the week from after the `W`, so the weekly path is read as intended
details: Observed in results/run1/weekly_workspace/inspection.txt: the last training workspace of the weekly reference run, downloaded through chapkit's artifact API by scripts/fetch_last_workspace.py. data.csv, historic.csv and future.csv all carry `time_period` as `2004-W01` … `2017-W52`; the date ranges of the source CSV (`2003-12-29/2004-01-04`) are not what the model sees. CH-06 stays as raised; this entry records its resolution.

challenge: Two behaviours of predict.R/lib.R on weekly data that the Python port must reproduce: it predicts every row with missing cases, and it folds ISO week 53 into the 52-week cycle
solution: To read in full and decide in batch 3 (translation inventory); recorded here because the reference run is where they were first observed
details: In the weekly workspace (results/run1/weekly_workspace/workspace/), predictions.csv has 60 rows: the 30 future rows (2017-W50..W52) plus 30 for the three historic periods with missing disease_cases (2008-W52, 2014-W52, 2016-W08). chap keeps only the future periods (external_chapkit_model.py, the start_timestamp mask in predict), so the scores are unaffected, but the Python service must return the same row set or chap's filtering must be relied on knowingly. historic.csv contains 30 rows of ISO week 53; lib.R's offset_years_and_weeks computes ((week + diff - 1) %% 52) + 1, which puts week 53 on the same cyclic index as another week.

challenge: INLA's default prior on the negative-binomial size is pc.mgamma(λ=7) on log size, not a log-gamma prior, and this INLA version ships no documentation page for it
solution: Ported from its C source: priorfunc_pc_mgamma evaluates the PC-gamma prior at a = exp(-theta) (inlaprog/src/inla-priors.c:1666-1696); read from inla.models() of the installed package
details: results/inla_defaults.tsv: nbinomial theta (size): prior 'pc.mgamma', parameter 7, initial log(10). Archive/r-sources/r-inla/src/r-inla.org/doc/prior/ has pc.gamma.tex but no pc.mgamma.tex. A port written from memory or from older INLA documentation would use another prior. The C function is short and is ported in batch 7, checked against INLA's own prior evaluation.

challenge: INLA's posterior predictive samples pass through engine layers that have no Python counterpart and are only specified by source code
solution: To decide per candidate in batches 7-10 (JC-13); recorded here so the decision is visible
details: inla.posterior.sample defaults (posterior.sample.R:375-379): use.improved.mean=TRUE (means from the VB correction, control.vb enable 'auto'), skew.corr=TRUE (skew-normal correction of the Gaussian samples). Hyperparameters are drawn from the integration configurations with probability proportional to exp(log posterior), without the integration weights (posterior.sample.R:488-496). Latent samples come from N(mean, Q^-1) at each configuration under the constraints (inla.qsample). inla.mode defaults to 'compact'; num.threads to '8:1'.

challenge: INLA silently sets missing fixed-effect covariate values to 0
solution: Reproduced in the Python data layer (batch 6): the NA rows of the cross-basis (the first nlag rows of each location) enter the fit as zeros
details: inla.R:794-802 (inla.na.action) replaces NA in numeric covariates by 0 before building the fixed-effect design matrix. predict.R never removes those rows, so they are in the fit with a zero basis contribution. A Python port that dropped them, or that let NaN propagate, would fit different data.

challenge: Resolution of CH-05 (sf and spdep loaded but apparently unused)
solution: Confirmed unused: no call in predict.R, lib.R or train.R resolves to sf, spdep or jsonlite; yaml (yaml.load_file) and dplyr (mutate) are used
details: results/r_calls.tsv, column supplied_by. The Python port needs no spatial-geometry library. CH-05 stays as raised; this entry records its resolution.

challenge: Resolution of CH-13 (weekly quirks: NA-case rows predicted, ISO week 53 folded)
solution: Both reproduced by the port (JC-11); the extra predicted rows are kept so the service returns what R returns, and chap's filtering does the rest as it does for R
details: CH-13 stays as raised; this entry records the decision.

challenge: Whether INLA's `Predictor` in the posterior samples includes the log(E) offset
solution: Source says yes (posterior.sample.R:437-440, the compact-mode path adds the offsets); to confirm numerically in batch 4 from the instrumented fit
details: predict.R draws rnbinom(mu = exp(Predictor)), which is the NB mean only if the offset is included. If it were not, the R reference's samples would be on a per-unit-population scale, and the port must match whichever is true. The batch-4 harness compares exp(Predictor) with E*exp(eta) on the fitted rows.

challenge: The R reference's INLA fit is not reproducible: identical inputs give different posteriors, occasionally a degenerate mode, occasionally a crash
solution: Recorded, not worked around; reported to the human before batch 5 sets tolerances (plan §3, stop and report)
details: Evidence, all in analysis/03_referenceHarness/results/. (1) Across 5 refits of each dataset x variant on byte-identical model frames, the posterior mode of the cyclic-RW1 log precision ranges over 1.77-2.04 (monthly default), 1.43-1.70 (monthly no_covariates), 2.65-2.85 (weekly nlags_3_6); the NB log size and iid log precision vary far less (fit_summary.tsv, refit_agreement.tsv). Monthly fitted values differ by up to 472 cases between refits. (2) One of 42 sweep fits (monthly default, the seeded repeat of replicate 1) converged to a degenerate mode: NB size 1.34, iid precision 290, 4 integration points instead of 15, six 'vb.correction aborted' warnings, mode_status 0 (seeded_repeat.tsv). (3) Three single-threaded fits per dataset (thread_diagnostic/) also differ from one another; on weekly data one crashed ('The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge') and two converged to degenerate modes. Threading is therefore not the cause. (4) Through chap, monthly repeat 1 produced no evaluation: INLA crashed with the same Newton-Raphson error in one backtest split (chap_repeats/service_container.log). Untested candidate causes: randomness inside INLA's optimiser or its rescue paths; the amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon (no native amd64 host was available). Consequences: the L3 noise floor is not a small numerical tolerance but a spread with occasional gross outliers; and an R-vs-R comparison at L3-L5 has to decide whether a degenerate R fit is part of the reference's behaviour or excluded from it — a decision for the human.

challenge: The host slept during the run, so wall-clock timings include sleep
solution: run.sh now wraps the long steps in caffeinate -i; the batch-4 timings are kept and marked as upper bounds; per-run cost for phase D is to be taken from the fits' INLA-internal fit_seconds or re-measured
details: pmset log shows maintenance sleeps between 22:31 and 22:48 local time during the sweep; one fit reports fit_seconds 306.9 inside a 38 s container run, which is only possible across a sleep of the Docker VM's clock.

challenge: CH-19 resolved: INLA's Predictor includes the log(E) offset
solution: Confirmed numerically in every fit: Predictor minus the linear predictor rebuilt from one posterior draw's components equals log(E) to at most 1.2e-14 (47 fits, fit_summary.tsv)
details: The same check confirms three things the Python port depends on: iid with replicate=ID_year indexes value j of replicate r at (r-1)*n + j; the region-specific cyclic RW1 with replicate=ID_spat indexes the same way; and missing basis values enter the linear predictor as 0 (CH-16).

challenge: The human's answer to CH-20: no tolerance and no pass/fail; the R reference counts as it runs
solution: Batch 5 describes closeness at every layer and labels every R fit's health; flagged fits and crashes are counted and shown, not excluded (plan §4b, 2026-10-17)
details: Of the 42 sweep fits, 41 are clean and 1 flagged (monthly default, the seeded repeat). Of the 6 single-threaded diagnostic fits, 3 are clean (monthly), 2 flagged and 1 crashed (weekly). Of 5 monthly chap evaluations, 1 crashed (analysis/04_fidelityMetrics/results/r_fit_health_counts.tsv, l5_evaluations.tsv).

challenge: A replicated random effect lists its IDs once per replicate, so matching two runs on ID pairs every replicate with every other
solution: Random-effect values are matched on their position, INLA's internal index (r-1)n+j (CH-22), with the ID kept for reading
details: Found on the first R-vs-R run: the iid term's shifts between clean refits came out at a median of 3 posterior sds; keyed by position they are 0.006 or less.

challenge: pandas' default CSV float parser is not round-trip exact
solution: Every CSV is read with float_precision='round_trip', as R's read.csv parses; the frame then matches R's exactly
details: With the default parser, population (and so E and the offset) differed from R's by up to 3.7e-9 on the monthly data.

challenge: Two INLA implementations of scale.model differ in the 8th digit
solution: The port follows the C library (gmrflib/rw.c GMRFLib_rw_scale, which adds sqrt(DBL_EPSILON) to the diagonal before inverting); R's inla.scale.model is used only as a cross-check
details: Scaling factors for 12, 52 and 53 nodes agree with R's inla.scale.model to 1.3e-8 relative (analysis/05_pythonModel/02_modelPrimitives/results/primitives_check.tsv).

challenge: The Docker daemon was not running at the start of the session
solution: Started by the agent (open -a Docker); needed for the INLA checks in the reference image and the Python service image

challenge: NUTS mixed slowly on the weekly data: in short test runs, min ESS 14-50 and R-hat up to 1.21, and up to 15 minutes for 450 iterations, against an ~8 h estimate for the planned run
solution: Reparametrised intercept and iid effect so the sampler moves along the direction the likelihood cannot see (JC-33); the same density, re-checked. The cross-basis coefficients remain the slowest-mixing quantities
details: The diagnosis (a ridge between intercept and mean iid effect) was the agent's hypothesis, borne out by the timing test rather than shown directly; the centred version stays selectable in mcmc_nuts.Target

challenge: The human's answer to CH-03 (no data-specific licence for the example datasets), re-checked by /release check before the v0.1.0 Zenodo release
solution: Released as is, on the human's decision: the datasets are public example data shipped openly in the GPL-3.0/AGPL-3.0 repositories chapkit_ewars_model and chap-core, and NOTICE states that this repository grants no licence for them
details: Options put to the human: (1) release as is; (2) ask the CHAP team for written confirmation first; (3) leave the data out and reference the upstream commits, which would also remove it from the analysis results. The human chose (1). The data are region-by-period aggregates (disease cases, rainfall, temperature, population), not personal data. The same check found no secrets in any of the 9,250 blobs in the history and no credential files; every source under Archive/ carries a redistributable licence (GPL, AGPL or MIT; pyinla is represented only by PyPI's public metadata).
